A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPOT research, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The main sections closely correspond. v1 ends after its references; v2 adds supplementary Sections 6–8, which are fully available for comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original tracking evaluations on CVO, TAP-Vid, and RoboTAP, together with efficiency measurements and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds causal baseline evaluations, attention ablations, efficiency measurements, temporal analyses, and qualitative failure cases in its supplement.

M1.justification: The memory-reading module, sensory memory, visibility-guided splatting, flow decoder, and warm-start procedure remain unchanged. Feature symbols are renamed, and Section 6 supplies architecture and loss details without establishing a redesign of the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions train on Kubric-CVO and Kubric-MOVi-F and evaluate on CVO, TAP-Vid's DAVIS/Kinetics/RGB-Stacking datasets, and RoboTAP. The supplement analyzes existing coverage through alternative protocols, temporal intervals, resolutions, and selected cases; it introduces no new dataset, domain, or tracking task.

E2.justification: Section 7 adds Track-On and DELTA to measured speed and memory comparisons. Table 5 also extends online comparator coverage through causal executions of TAPIR, CoTracker2, SpatialTracker, and DOT with their original window sizes. The original benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds causal evaluation that repeatedly supplies available video prefixes while preserving baseline window sizes, alongside the retained two-frame-window protocol. It also adds resolution sweeps and interval-specific DAVIS evaluation. Section 6 specifies 32 decoding iterations for Kinetics, RGB-Stacking, and RoboTAP, exceptions absent from v1's stated 16-iteration default; this changes the documented settings without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, Table 6 tests backward propagation without attention-based retrieval. Figures 7–10 add resolution scaling, accuracy versus temporal interval, a qualitative memory-bank ablation, and analysis of recovery after occlusion exceeding memory length. Figure 13 adds explicit failure cases involving prolonged occlusion, similar textureless objects, and fast motion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The added tables and curves continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain identical numerical entries. New results include Table 5's causal DAVIS comparisons and Table 6's attention ablation, where CVO Extended EPE is 395.35 versus 6.42 for SPOT within that experiment. v2 also adds resolution and temporal curves, Track-On/DELTA resource measurements, and qualitative recovery and failure findings.

T1.justification: The mathematical procedure in Equations 1–7 is retained apart from notation. The supplement spells out the existing bilinear kernel and loss implementation, but adds no substantive theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: streaming-memory online dense tracking, strong CVO and sparse-tracking performance, computational efficiency, and causal processing. The supplementary evidence supports these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v1 mainly warns that prolonged occlusion can make memory unhelpful and tracking fail. v2 explains effective pairwise behavior when memory becomes unavailable, illustrates recovery after a ten-frame occlusion, and documents additional failure conditions. It also develops the interpretation that two-stage propagation and retrieval matter more than choosing forward splatting versus backward warping.

D1.justification: Section 6 supplies previously missing feature dimensions, encoder stride, mask-decoder details, bilinear-kernel formula, loss weighting, FlashAttention-2 usage, Adam with a one-cycle schedule, learning rate, batch sizes, and eight-H100 training hardware. These substantially improve implementation specificity. The abstract replaces the direct repository link with a project-page link, and the text points to animations; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Track-On, DELTA, FlashAttention-2, and the one-cycle training schedule. Section 7 distinguishes SPOT's online dense setting from Track-On's online sparse and DELTA's offline dense tracking. The main related-work discussion and broader novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved. Local edits rename feature notation, separate Discussion and Limitation paragraphs, add supplementary cross-references and acknowledgements, and append Sections 6–8. These additions do not constitute an extensive rewrite or reorganization of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 retains the original figures and tables, with small notation and caption changes to Figure 3. It adds Tables 5–6 and Figures 7–13, including resolution and temporal plots, memory-ablation images, an occlusion timeline, expanded qualitative comparisons, and failure-case grids. This substantially expands the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important reproducibility and validation gaps in v1. Section 6 supplies essential architecture, loss, and training specifications; Table 5 tests online comparisons without shrinking baseline windows; and the added memory analyses and failure cases strengthen the evidence for the mechanism while clarifying its limits. Together these substantially improve the paper's assessability and experimental support, even though the main benchmark scores remain unchanged.
